summary: Finite-field Diffie-Hellman in the TLS handshake has security, interoperability and efficiency shortcomings from unclear rules about which group parameters servers offer and clients accept. This standards-track RFC uses part of the TLS Supported Groups extension to negotiate named groups.

eli5.summary: Rather than a server picking its own secret numbers, both sides agree on a well-known set from a list.

questions: what is the tls supported groups extension
subtitle: Named finite-field Diffie-Hellman groups that let TLS clients and servers agree on safe key-exchange parameters.

tldr.problem: In TLS, a server picks its own Diffie-Hellman group, and the client cannot say what it can handle or easily check that the group is safe, so it can only accept or hang up.
tldr.mechanism: Five named groups (ffdhe2048 to ffdhe8192) are added to the Supported Groups extension, the client lists the ones it accepts, and the server MUST pick one of them.
tldr.outcome: Both sides know the group has a safe-prime structure, so a simple range check on the public key replaces expensive validation, and weak custom groups can be avoided.

facts.label: Minimum custom group
facts.value: MUST reject under 768 bits, SHOULD reject under 1024 bits

today: RFC 7919 is a Proposed Standard from August 2016. It updates RFC 2246, RFC 4346, RFC 4492 and RFC 5246, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DHE in TLS Needed Fixing
sections.content:
Traditional TLS (RFC 5246) has a Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (DHE) mode that gives forward secrecy. The server sends group parameters, a generator g and a modulus p. If the client thinks the group is weak, for example p is too small or not prime, it can only terminate the connection.

The server has the opposite problem. It does not know what groups the client handles, and some widely distributed clients cannot handle p above 1024 bits. A client also has no efficient way to check that an arbitrary p and g have a safe structure.

This RFC fixes this by reusing the Supported Groups registry and extension to negotiate common groups with known structure. It updates TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 and the TLS ECC extensions, and use against a non-compatible peer should have no detrimental effects.
sections.eli5: Before, the server handed over a recipe and the client could not tell if it was a good one. Now they agree on a recipe from a trusted list first.

sections.title: Named Groups
sections.content:
The existing elliptic_curves(10) extension is renamed the Supported Groups extension, and the NamedCurve type becomes NamedGroup. The client MAY send it when either FFDHE or ECDHE cipher suites are listed. Codepoints 256 to 511 are set aside for FFDHE groups, and five are defined: ffdhe2048(256), ffdhe3072(257), ffdhe4096(258), ffdhe6144(259) and ffdhe8192(260).

All are safe primes derived from the base of the natural logarithm, e, with the high and low 64 bits set to 1 for efficient reduction. Using e is a nothing-up-my-sleeve choice: the middle bits are effectively random, with no suspicion that the primes were chosen to be weak. The RFC does not reuse groups from other lists, such as IKE groups, partly because reusing the same groups in several protocols raises the value of cracking any one of them.
sections.eli5: The menu has five sizes of recipe. They were made from a famous number so nobody can claim the authors hid a trick inside.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
A compatible client sends the Supported Groups extension in the ClientHello with its FFDHE groups, most preferred first. If it also offers ECDHE, it MUST put every group in a single extension. It SHOULD also offer at least one FFDHE cipher suite, and it MUST be able and willing to use any group it offers.

When the server answers with an FFDHE suite, the client SHOULD validate the signature over the ServerDHParams and compare the chosen dh_p and dh_g with its offered groups. If nothing matches, the server is not compatible. The client MAY continue if local policy accepts the custom group, or end the connection with a fatal insufficient_security(71) alert. In any case the client MUST check 1 < dh_Ys < dh_p - 1, otherwise it ends with a fatal handshake_failure(40) alert.

For custom groups from non-compatible servers, a client MUST reject any group with |dh_p| under 768 bits and SHOULD reject any under 1024 bits.
sections.eli5: The client shows its favorite recipes in order. If the server picks something off the menu, the client checks it is acceptable and checks the answer is in a sensible range.

sections.title: Server Behavior
sections.content:
If the client lists any FFDHE group (codepoints 256 to 511) and none is known and acceptable to the server, the server MUST NOT select an FFDHE cipher suite. It SHOULD pick an acceptable non-FFDHE suite, and if none exists it MUST end the connection with a fatal insufficient_security(71) alert.

If an FFDHE suite is offered but the extension is missing or has no FFDHE groups, the client is not compatible. The server MAY then choose a non-FFDHE suite or use an FFDHE group of its own choice.

With a compatible client, a server that picks an FFDHE suite MUST choose one of the offered groups, MUST NOT select a named group the client did not offer, and MUST NOT select an FFDHE suite the client did not offer. It SHOULD pick a group at least as strong as its own public key: with a 3072-bit RSA key and a client offering only ffdhe2048 and ffdhe4096, it SHOULD choose ffdhe4096. When it receives the ClientKeyExchange, it MUST verify 1 < dh_Yc < dh_p - 1 or end with a fatal handshake_failure(40) alert.
sections.eli5: The server may only choose from the client's menu. If nothing on it works, the server picks another way to talk or hangs up politely.

sections.title: Optimizations
sections.content:
Because the group is a known safe prime, both peers know the group size is p-1 or (p-1)/2. This allows three optimizations.

  • Public key check: peers MUST confirm 1 < Y < p-1. Without a known group, a client would have to verify primality and factor p-1.
  • Short exponents: each group gives a lower bound on the secret exponent size. For ffdhe3072 a peer can pick an exponent of at least 275 bits instead of doing work proportional to 3072.
  • Table acceleration: precompute powers of the generator, trading memory for time. This speeds up only the first, fixed-base exponentiation.
sections.eli5: Because the recipes are known to be good, you can skip a lot of checking and use smaller secret numbers to go faster.

sections.title: Preference Ordering
sections.content:
The group list can mix ECDHE and FFDHE groups, ranked by client preference. The cipher suite list is also ranked, so the two can contradict each other. Clients SHOULD NOT present such a contradiction. A server that sees one SHOULD give priority to the Supported Groups extension, but MAY resolve it any way it sees fit.

Clients MAY interleave the two kinds, for example ffdhe8192, secp384p1, ffdhe3072, secp256r1, to prefer stronger groups regardless of cost while accepting weaker ones.
sections.eli5: If your two lists of favorites disagree, the group list wins, since it is the more specific one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Supported Groups contents are covered by the Finished message hash, so an active attacker who removes or edits groups makes the handshake fail, though possibly not before a peer has done something it would not otherwise have done. This matters for TLS False Start: clients doing a full handshake MUST NOT use False Start if the server picks an FFDHE suite with a group the client does not consider cryptographically strong.

Group strength matters because recorded sessions can be attacked later. The RFC cites a recommendation that future systems use FFDHE sizes of at least 3072 bits, and ffdhe3072 is intended for them. Implementations should use constant-time modular exponentiation, and forward secrecy requires discarding ephemeral keys promptly. The RFC also notes that ECDHE appears to offer a much stronger key exchange than FFDHE, and that revisions should mark weak groups as deprecated.

A client that accepts non-negotiated FFDHE groups remains exposed to premaster secret replay attacks, unless the session hash fix in RFC 7627 is used. On privacy, the extension gives a few additional bits for client fingerprinting.
sections.eli5: If a sneaky person tampers with the menu, the final check catches it. Bigger recipes keep secrets safe for longer, and you should throw away your secret numbers when finished.

messages.label: ClientHello
messages.note: Supported Groups lists FFDHE groups, plus at least one FFDHE cipher suite.

messages.label: ServerKeyExchange
messages.note: Carries one of the offered groups and dh_Ys.

messages.label: ClientKeyExchange
messages.note: Carries dh_Yc; the server checks it is in range.
